updates.title: The bias-testing exception moved from Article 10(5) to Article 4a, and now reaches deployers
updates.was: Article 10(5) creates a limited exception to GDPR's prohibition on processing special category data. Providers of high-risk AI may process this data for bias detection and correction.
updates.now: Article 4a creates the exception. Until July 2026 it was Article 10(5) and covered only providers of high-risk AI. The amendment moved it to Article 4a and opened it, on the same six conditions, to deployers of high-risk AI and to providers and deployers of other AI systems and models. Deletion is due once the bias is corrected or the retention period ends, whichever comes first.
sources: Art. 1(6) inserts Art. 4a; Art. 1(9)(b) deletes Art. 10(5)

updates.title: Data origin is Article 10(2)(b), not "(aa)"
updates.was: Data provenance (Art. 10(2)(aa))
updates.now: Data provenance (Art. 10(2)(b)). The letter "(aa)" came from a draft of the Act. In the published text Article 10(2) runs from (a) to (h), and origin of the data is point (b).

updates.title: One name for the checking layer: AI-Mart
updates.was: "Feature Mart quality gates" and "The Feature Mart becomes the compliance enforcement point."
updates.now: "AI-Mart quality gates" and "The AI-Mart becomes the compliance enforcement point." Chapter 9 calls this layer the AI-Mart; the site now uses that one name everywhere.
updates.where: Article 10 to Data Vault table; key concept quote

updates.title: When Article 10 starts to apply
updates.was: Nothing on timing.
updates.now: The high-risk rules, Article 10 included, apply from 2 December 2027 for the stand-alone uses listed in Annex III and from 2 August 2028 for AI built into regulated products.

updates.title: The ePrivacy Regulation was not withdrawn in February 2025: that was the announcement
updates.was: The ePrivacy Regulation was formally withdrawn by the EU Commission in February 2025.
updates.now: It was withdrawn in 2025, in three steps. On 11 February 2025 the Commission announced that it intended to withdraw the proposal. On 16 July 2025 it approved the withdrawal. On 6 October 2025 the withdrawal was published in the Official Journal. The ePrivacy Directive of 2002 is still in force.
updates.where: ePrivacy section, layer 4; comparison table; "On ePrivacy" quote; fold-out note; Exercise 2, statement 3
sources: closing sentence: approved at the 2533rd meeting, 16 July 2025

updates.title: The Digital Omnibus on data is still a proposal
updates.was: The Commission proposed a "Digital Omnibus" package in late 2025 that may fold some ePrivacy territory into a broader legislative revision. Whether this succeeds is genuinely uncertain.
updates.now: The proposal (COM(2025) 837, 19 November 2025) would move the cookie rules for personal data into the GDPR. It is not law. The Council agreed its negotiating position on 21 October 2026, and that position keeps the cookie rules in the ePrivacy Directive. The European Parliament has not adopted a position, so talks between the two have not started. The separate Digital Omnibus on AI did become law (see chapter 9).
sources: "maintains the rules on cookies ... under the e-privacy directive"

updates.title: "In force" and "applies" are two different dates
updates.was: A table row labelled "In force" gave May 2018 (GDPR), Sep 2025 (Data Act) and Jan 2025 (DORA). A note said the Data Governance Act was "in force Sep 2023" and the Data Act "in force Sep 2025".
updates.now: The row is labelled "Applies since". Those are the dates from which the rules must be followed. Each law entered into force earlier: GDPR on 24 May 2016 (applies 25 May 2018), DORA on 16 January 2023 (applies 17 January 2025), the Data Act on 11 January 2024 (applies 12 September 2025), the Data Governance Act on 23 June 2022 (applies 24 September 2023).
updates.where: comparison table; fold-out note on the Data Governance Act

updates.title: Data Act: what happens on 12 September 2027
updates.was: Sep 12, 2027: Contractual terms for B2B data sharing; full enforcement
updates.now: On 12 September 2027 the rules against unfair contract terms (Chapter IV) start to cover older contracts: those signed on or before 12 September 2025 that are open-ended or run until at least 11 January 2034. Contracts signed after 12 September 2025 are covered from the start. The other two dates on the page (12 September 2025 and 12 September 2026) were checked and are right.

updates.title: DORA article numbers
updates.was: Article 6: register of ICT assets. Article 17: classify and report incidents. Article 25: testing, including TLPT. "The CTPP framework (Articles 28-44)". "DORA Art. 6" in the lineage table.
updates.now: Article 8 (identification) is the duty to identify and document ICT assets and their dependencies; Article 6 is the overall risk framework. Incidents: Articles 17 to 19 (reporting is Article 19). Testing: Articles 24 to 26 (threat-led penetration testing is Article 26). The oversight framework for critical providers is Articles 31 to 44; Articles 28 to 30 are the general third-party risk rules.
updates.where: DORA section, layers 3 and 4; lineage table

updates.title: The first critical ICT providers have been named
updates.was: AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud are likely among the first designees.
updates.now: The European Supervisory Authorities published the first list on 18 November 2025: 19 companies, among them Amazon Web Services EMEA, Microsoft Ireland Operations and Google Cloud EMEA.
sources: press release and list under DORA Art. 31(9)

updates.title: The adequacy list now includes Brazil and the European Patent Organisation
updates.was: Currently adequate: Andorra, Argentina, Canada (commercial), Faroe Islands, Guernsey, Israel, Isle of Man, Japan, Jersey, New Zealand, Republic of Korea, Switzerland, UK, Uruguay, and the US under the DPF.
updates.now: The same list plus Brazil (adequacy decision of 26 January 2026) and one international body, the European Patent Organisation (15 July 2025). The UK decisions were renewed on 19 December 2025 and now run until 27 December 2031.

updates.title: Exercise 1: the Brazil scenario now uses India
updates.was: "A French startup sends analytics data to a cloud provider in Brazil." Expected answer: standard contractual clauses with a transfer impact assessment.
updates.now: The scenario names India. Brazil has had an adequacy decision since 26 January 2026, so the expected answer would have been wrong. India has no adequacy decision, so the expected answer stays the same.
sources: India is not on the list

updates.title: EU-US Data Privacy Framework: still valid; first challenge dismissed, appeal pending
updates.was: Currently valid for certified US organizations. "Schrems III?": NOYB has indicated it will challenge the DPF. Status: Challenge Expected.
updates.now: The framework is still valid on 20 November 2026. On 3 September 2025 the EU General Court dismissed the first challenge (T-553/23, Latombe v Commission). The appeal to the Court of Justice (C-703/25 P, lodged 31 October 2025) is pending: no Advocate General opinion and no judgment yet. NOYB has not filed a case so far; on 29 June 2026 it announced that it would, after the US Supreme Court ruled in Trump v. Slaughter that the President may dismiss FTC commissioners. On 31 July 2026 the European Data Protection Board asked the Commission to assess whether that ruling affects the framework.
updates.where: Schrems timeline, last two entries; key concept quote
sources: "will also file a lawsuit in the coming weeks"

updates.title: The EU cloud certification scheme is still not adopted
updates.was: The EU Cybersecurity Certification Scheme for Cloud Services is debating whether the highest certification level should require EU ownership and control.
updates.now: The scheme has still not been adopted. In June 2026 the Commission wrote that certification can cover technical security but is not suited to sovereignty questions, and proposed to deal with those in a separate law, the Cloud and AI Development Act, which is itself only a proposal.

updates.title: DORA: asset mapping is Article 8, not Article 6
updates.was: DORA, Art. 6: map information assets, identify dependencies, document data flows
updates.now: DORA, Art. 8 (identification). Article 6 is the overall ICT risk management framework. Same correction as in chapter 7.

updates.title: Social scoring is banned for everyone, not only for governments
updates.was: Social scoring by a government (rating citizens' behavior to restrict services) is banned outright. Quiz feedback said the Act bans social scoring "by public authorities".
updates.now: The ban in Article 5(1)(c) covers any AI system that scores people on their social behaviour or personal traits and then treats them worse in an unrelated setting or out of proportion. It applies to public bodies and private companies alike. The feedback texts of Exercise 1 were corrected to match.

updates.title: Two more banned practices from 2 December 2026
updates.was: "Article 5 prohibitions are already in force since Feb 2025." Nothing on the two new bans, which did not exist yet.
updates.now: The Article 5 bans have applied since 2 February 2025. Two more start on 2 December 2026: AI that creates or alters realistic intimate or sexually explicit images, video or audio of an identifiable person without consent, and AI that generates child sexual abuse material.
sources: Art. 5(1)(ba) and (bb); Art. 113, third paragraph, point (a)

updates.title: High-risk obligations start on 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028
updates.was: Annex III high-risk obligations: August 2026. Product-embedded AI: August 2027. Financial services clients "must comply a full year before" manufacturing clients.
updates.now: Annex III systems: 2 December 2027. AI in regulated products (Annex I): 2 August 2028. The gap between the two is eight months. The earlier dates were right when the chapter was written: they were the dates in the original 2024 text. The timeline table has four new rows (27 July 2026, 2 December 2026, 2 December 2027, 2 August 2028).
updates.where: Risk tiers, layer 3; enforcement timeline table
sources: Art. 113, third paragraph, point (c); Art. 111(3) and (4)

updates.title: The product-safety list is Annex I, not Annex II
updates.was: Annex II (product safety): AI embedded in already-regulated products.
updates.now: Annex I lists the EU product-safety laws (medical devices, machinery, toys, vehicles). Annex II is a list of criminal offences used for one of the Article 5 bans. "Annex II" for product safety was draft numbering.
updates.where: Risk tiers, layer 3; timeline table; radiology example

updates.title: The Digital Omnibus on AI is law
updates.was: Digital Omnibus proposal (Nov 2025): the Commission proposed delaying Annex III enforcement by up to 16 months. Not yet adopted. Clients are in limbo: the enforcement timeline is shifting.
updates.now: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 was published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026 and entered into force on 27 July 2026. It set fixed dates for the high-risk obligations, reworded Article 4, moved the bias-testing exception to a new Article 4a and added two banned practices. The timeline is no longer shifting.
sources: Art. 4 (entry into force on the third day after publication)

updates.title: Germany's implementing law (KI-MIG) is in force
updates.was: Germany's Federal Cabinet approved the KI-MIG in February 2026, designating the Bundesnetzagentur as primary AI market surveillance authority, though the law is still completing its parliamentary process.
updates.now: The Bundestag passed the law on 11 June 2026. It was published on 28 July 2026 and has applied since 29 July 2026. The Bundesnetzagentur is the market surveillance authority, the single point of contact and the complaints office. BaFin and the existing product-safety authorities keep their own sectors.

updates.title: What the 3% fine tier is tied to
updates.was: High-risk non-compliance (Arts. 9-15): EUR 15,000,000 or 3%
updates.now: The 15 million / 3% tier in Article 99(4) is tied to the duties of each kind of operator: providers (Article 16), authorised representatives, importers, distributors, deployers (Article 26), notified bodies, and the transparency duties of Article 50. Articles 9 to 15 come in through Article 16, which makes providers responsible for meeting them. The amounts were checked and are right.

updates.title: Data origin is Article 10(2)(b), not "(aa)"
updates.was: Data provenance: 10(2)(aa)
updates.now: Data provenance: 10(2)(b). "(aa)" was draft lettering; the published Article 10(2) runs from (a) to (h).

updates.title: One name for the checking layer: AI-Mart
updates.was: Validation gates at AI-Mart / Feature Mart
updates.now: Validation gates at AI-Mart. The site now uses one name for this layer.
updates.where: Article 10 mapping, layer 3; Exercise 2 worked example

updates.title: Article 10(5) was deleted; the rule is now Article 4a and reaches deployers
updates.was: Article 10(5) opens a narrow door: you can process special category data for bias detection. Article 10(5) is the legal basis.
updates.now: Article 4a(1) carries the same six conditions that Article 10(5) had, for providers of high-risk systems. Article 4a(2) opens the same door, on the same conditions, to deployers of high-risk systems and to providers and deployers of other AI systems and models, and creates no duty to run such tests. Recital 9 of the amending regulation ties the exception to GDPR Art. 9(2)(g); whether it can stand alone as a legal basis is still debated among scholars.

updates.title: AI literacy (Article 4) was reworded
updates.was: Applies to all AI systems. Already in effect since Feb 2025. No standalone fine, but non-compliance is an aggravating factor. For BI consultants, understanding the AI Act is a legal obligation.
updates.now: Providers and deployers must take measures to support the development of AI literacy of their staff and of others who operate AI on their behalf. The text now says this does not require guaranteeing any specific level of AI literacy for any individual. Article 99 sets no fine of its own for Article 4. The sentence about an "aggravating factor" was removed: the Act does not say that. The sentence that called AI Act knowledge a legal obligation for consultants was softened: the duty in Article 4 falls on providers and deployers.

updates.title: The radiology example is high-risk as a medical device, not as biometrics
updates.was: High Risk (Annex III Domain 1, Biometrics / Annex II if embedded in a medical device)
updates.now: High Risk through Article 6(1) and Annex I: the software is a medical device, or a safety part of one, under Regulation (EU) 2017/745 and needs a third-party conformity assessment. Reading a scan does not identify or categorise people, so Annex III point 1 (biometrics) is not the route.
sources: Art. 6(1); Annex I, Section A, point 11; Annex III, point 1

updates.title: Human oversight: Article 14 for the system, Article 26(2) for the deployer
updates.was: Under AI Act Article 14: the deployer must implement human oversight.
updates.now: Article 14 requires the system to be designed so that people can oversee it; that is a requirement on the product, met by the provider. Article 26(2) is the deployer's duty: assign oversight to people with the competence, training and authority to do it.
updates.where: Dual compliance, card 2; Exercise 3 worked example and reference answer

updates.title: Article 10(3) is now quoted word for word
updates.was: "The high-risk AI system shall use data that is relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible, free of errors."
updates.now: "Training, validation and testing data sets shall be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose." (Art. 10(3))

updates.title: The transparency duties apply since 2 August 2026
updates.was: Nothing on timing.
updates.now: Article 50 (tell people they are talking to an AI; label deepfakes and AI-generated content) has applied since 2 August 2026. Generative systems placed on the market before that date have until 2 December 2026 to mark their output.

updates.title: The self-test now holds the questions it announces: 15, all with a model answer
updates.was: The page said "All 20 questions answered" but held 7 cards. Two of them (M2, M9) had no model answer, the scorecard listed two trap questions (M4, M7) that were not on the page, and the test could never be completed. The question cards also showed without their styling: a cut-off line in the page's stylesheet made browsers ignore everything after it.
updates.now: 15 questions: four calibration questions, then M1 to M11. M3 to M8, M10 and M11 were written new; M2 and M9 received their model answers. The five career questions of the original version were removed before the site went public and stay out. The stylesheet is repaired, so the cards, buttons and trap reveals look as designed. The answers reflect the law as of 20 November 2026 (for example, the bias-testing rule is cited as AI Act Article 4a).
updates.where: Sections "Technical compliance" and "Integration and edge cases"; closing line; progress logic; the page's stylesheet

updates.title: Telling recipients about an erasure is GDPR Article 19
updates.was: If data was shared with third parties, notify them (Art. 17(2)).
updates.now: The duty to tell each recipient the data was disclosed to is Article 19. Article 17(2) covers a narrower case: data the controller made public.

updates.title: One set of names for the three sovereignty questions
updates.was: Physical location, legal jurisdiction, operational control.
updates.now: Legal (whose laws apply), infrastructure (who owns and runs the servers), political (can a foreign government demand access): the names chapter 8 teaches. The same wording is now in the inventory item "Data Sovereignty (3D)".
updates.where: Calibration question 2, model answer; inventory text

unchanged.claim: The AI Act is Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 and entered into force on 1 August 2024.
Fines: up to EUR 35 million or 7% for banned practices; EUR 15 million or 3%; EUR 7.5 million or 1% for incorrect information.
Serious incidents: report within 15 days; 2 days for a widespread infringement or a serious disruption of critical infrastructure. (Also in the Act: 10 days where a person has died.)
The eight Annex III areas and the examples given for each, including targeted job advertising under employment and credit scoring under essential services.
Obligations for general-purpose AI models apply since 2 August 2025; models already on the market have until 2 August 2027.
Article 10(6): for systems that are not trained on data, the data rules apply to the testing data sets only.
DORA applies from 17 January 2025 and entered into force in January 2023.

Data Act: most rules apply from 12 September 2025; the design duty for new connected products from 12 September 2026; cloud switching is Articles 23 to 31; fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory terms are in Article 8.
GDPR fines: up to EUR 20 million or 4% (Art. 83(5)); EUR 10 million or 2% (Art. 83(4)). Applies since 25 May 2018.
Schrems I (C-362/14, 6 October 2015) struck down Safe Harbour; Schrems II (C-311/18, 16 July 2020) struck down Privacy Shield and kept standard contractual clauses.
unchanged.pin: C-311/18 on EUR-Lex; Schrems I is C-362/14

unchanged.claim: The CLOUD Act (2018) reaches data in a provider's "possession, custody, or control" wherever it is stored.
Whether the EU-based sovereign cloud offerings are out of reach of the CLOUD Act has not been tested in an EU court: no ruling was found on 20 November 2026.
unchanged.pin: no EU court ruling on this point was found

unchanged.claim: Japan's adequacy decision covers private-sector business operators; the US decision covers certified organisations only.
